items.title: Drought-severity forecasts translate into the 2026 Glen Canyon Dam release decision
items.operational_question: How do Lake Powell inflow forecasts and elevation-tier classification, through the Interim Guidelines' four-tier structure and the DROA, translate into an annual Glen Canyon Dam release decision such as the 2026 reduction?
items.synthesis_claim: A near-record-low WY2026 inflow forecast was classified through the CRSS/24-Month Study process into the Mid-Elevation Release Tier band, which triggered the 2024 SEIS ROD's Section 6.E emergency-reduction authority once the minimum-probable study projected Lake Powell below 3,500 ft; Interior then set the WY2026 release at 6.00 maf (down from the tier's default 7.48 maf) and paired it with a DROA-triggered supplemental release from Flaming Gorge Reservoir, publicly announced through Reclamation's April 2026 newsroom release.
items.scope_and_conditions: Water Year 2026 Glen Canyon Dam operations, as reflected in the Draft 2026 Annual Operating Plan and the July 2026 Most Probable 24-Month Study; the Draft AOP is not yet a finalized document.

analysis_chain.statement: WY2026 unregulated inflow was forecast near-record-low: 3.50 maf (36% of the 1991-2020 average) in the July 2026 Most Probable 24-Month Study, with the April 2026 minimum-probable case at 2.78 maf (29% of average), one of the lowest on record.

Running this forecast through the 24-Month Study/CRSS workflow places Lake Powell within the Mid-Elevation Release Tier band (elevation 3,525-3,575 ft) and flags the DROA's 3,525 ft target elevation as at risk, with the April study additionally projecting a decline below the 3,490 ft minimum power pool absent intervention.

The Mid-Elevation Release Tier's default 7.48 maf rule (2007 Interim Guidelines Section 6.C) is overridden for WY2026 by Section 6.E of the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS ROD, which authorizes a reduced release once the minimum-probable 24-Month Study projects Lake Powell below elevation 3,500 feet.

The Department of the Interior implemented Section 6.E to reduce Lake Powell's WY2026 annual release from 7.48 maf to 6.00 maf, and paired this with a DROA-triggered 660,000 acre-foot to 1 maf supplemental release from Flaming Gorge Reservoir into Lake Powell (April 2026-April 2027), agreed to by the four Upper Basin states.

Reclamation announced and documented the combined release-reduction and Flaming-Gorge-release package through its April 2026 newsroom release and the Draft 2026 Annual Operating Plan, framing it as an unprecedented action to protect Glen Canyon Dam's water-delivery and hydropower infrastructure.

supporting_evidence.summary: Observed unregulated inflow into Lake Powell for June 2026 was 0.306 maf (12% of the 1991-2020 average); the July 2026 forecast is only 0.020 maf (2% of average), and the April-July 2026 forecast is 1.08 maf (17% of average), while the full WY2026 unregulated inflow forecast is 3.50 maf (36% of average).

supporting_evidence.summary: The Interim Guidelines for Coordinated Operations of Lake Powell and Lake Mead define four operating tiers -- the Equalization Tier, Upper Elevation Balancing Tier, Mid-Elevation Release Tier, and Lower Elevation Balancing Tier -- with scheduled Lake Powell water-year releases adjusted each month based on forecast inflow and projected September 30 elevations at both reservoirs. In CRSS modeling of the Continued Current Strategies baseline, each January's governing tier is set by end-of-calendar-year pool elevation: the Equalization Tier applies at or above the Equalization Level; the Upper Elevation Balancing Tier applies down to elevation 3,575 feet; the Mid-Elevation Release Tier applies between 3,575 and 3,525 feet; and the Lower Elevation Balancing Tier applies below elevation 3,525 feet.

Under the 2007 Interim Guidelines' Mid-Elevation Release Tier (Section 6.C), when the projected January 1 Lake Powell elevation is below 3,575 feet and at or above 3,525 feet, the Secretary releases 7.48 maf from Lake Powell in the Water Year if the projected January 1 Lake Mead elevation is at or above 1,025 feet (or 8.23 maf if Lake Mead is below 1,025 feet). Both the Draft 2026 Annual Operating Plan and the July 2026 Most Probable 24-Month Study confirm this Mid-Elevation Release Tier (per 2007 Interim Guidelines Section 6.C.1 and the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS ROD Section 6.E) governs Lake Powell operations for Water Year 2026, with the August 2025 24-Month Study's most probable inflow scenario originally projecting a 7.48 maf release from Glen Canyon Dam for WY2026.

Reclamation's '24-Month Study' is the recurring monthly operational model that projects Colorado River reservoir levels 24 months into the future to inform near-term operating decisions, with each monthly run modeling a single scenario of reservoir conditions. Operationally, projected monthly inflow volumes from probabilistic hydrologic scenarios are input into the 24-Month Study, and the resulting projected monthly releases for each system reservoir are adjusted from the prior month's 24-Month Study baseline until release and storage levels best accomplish project purposes and operational objectives.

Under the Upper Basin DCP's DROA, Upper Basin states agreed to operate system units to keep Lake Powell's surface above elevation 3,525 feet, 35 feet above minimum power pool (EU-LP-CRS-001-04). Reclamation's stated operational goal under DROA is to 'protect' this 3,525-ft elevation, primarily via reduced Glen Canyon Dam releases and drawdown of upstream initial-unit reservoirs (EU-LP-CRS-002-04). The DROA establishes the process for Reclamation, in collaboration with the Upper Basin States, to release additional water from upstream CRSP initial-unit reservoirs (Flaming Gorge, Aspinall, Navajo, Glen Canyon/Lake Powell) to reduce the risk of Lake Powell reaching critical elevation (EU-LP-OFF-017-03). In CRSS modeling, Powell Infrastructure Protection (PIP) releases from the Upper Initial Units (Flaming Gorge, Blue Mesa, Navajo) are specifically triggered when Lake Powell is projected to fall below elevation 3,525 feet (EU-LP-OFF-021-06). This target was actually invoked when the July 2025 24-Month Study projected Lake Powell declining below the 3,525.00-ft DROA target elevation, triggering DROA year-2025 drought-response planning under the DCP-related agreements (EU-LP-OFF-022-03); consistent with protecting this same target, the December 2025 24-Month Study reduced Glen Canyon Dam's monthly release volumes for December 2025 through April 2026 by 0.598 maf (EU-LP-OFF-023-03).

On April 17, 2026, the Bureau of Reclamation announced unprecedented actions to store more water in Lake Powell -- then less than 25 percent full -- to preserve hydropower generation and protect Glen Canyon Dam water-delivery infrastructure the agency said was at risk from low reservoir levels (EU-LP-MED-001-01). With the consent of the four Upper Basin states, Reclamation committed to releasing between 660,000 and 1 million acre-feet from Flaming Gorge Reservoir (82 percent full) into Lake Powell over the 12 months following the announcement, building on a smaller 463,000-acre-foot release used to prop up Powell in 2022-23 (EU-LP-MED-001-02). Because WY2026 was historically dry and Lake Powell was projected to decline below elevation 3,500 feet, the Department of the Interior invoked Section 6.E of the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS ROD to reduce Lake Powell's annual release from 7.48 maf to 6.00 maf, coupled with a 2026 Drought Response Operations Plan releasing approximately 660,000 to 1.00 maf of additional water from Flaming Gorge Reservoir to Lake Powell by April 2027 (EU-LP-OFF-023-02). Reclamation's newsroom release confirms the combined plan: adding about 2.48 million acre-feet via the 660,000 AF-1 maf Flaming Gorge release (April 2026-April 2027, under the 2019 Drought Response Operating Agreements) plus the 7.48-to-6.0-maf release reduction through September 2026 under Section 6E, together expected to raise Lake Powell's elevation about 54 feet to at least 3,500 feet by April 2027 (EU-LP-OFF-035-02).

The July 2026 Most Probable 24-Month Study reports the full WY2026 unregulated inflow forecast for Lake Powell as 3.50 maf, 36 percent of the 1991-2020 average (OFF-023-05). The Lower Colorado Weekly Hydrologic Update dated July 27, 2026 reports the WY2026 unregulated inflow forecast as 3,501 kaf (36% of normal), an increase of 10 kaf from the previous forecast of 3,491 kaf (also 36% of normal) (OFF-024-02).

Circle of Blue reporting (April 2026) states inflows into Lake Powell in 2026 are projected to be the lowest ever measured, breaking the previous record set in 2002, driven by a downward snowpack trend and a March 2026 heat wave that was the most extreme on record in the Southwest for that time of year (MED-001-05). Reclamation's newsroom release states Lake Powell's water year 2026 minimum probable inflow is forecasted at just 2.78 million acre-feet, 29 percent of historical average and one of the lowest on record, with Reclamation's April 24-Month Study projecting Lake Powell may decline below 3,490 ft (minimum power pool) by August 2026 without major intervention (OFF-035-01).

items.uncertainty_or_exception: KC-LP-EMR-05 documents that 2021-2022 DROA-triggered upstream release volumes were reported at different acre-foot totals by CRS versus Reclamation's own DROA page; the 2026 package's figures should be read from Reclamation's own July 2026 24-Month Study and newsroom release rather than assumed reconcilable with every secondary account of past DROA actions.
items.operational_implication: A retrieval system answering 'why is the 2026 Glen Canyon release only 6.0 maf instead of 7.48 maf' should surface the full forecast-to-implementation chain (inflow forecast, tier classification, Section 6.E override, quantified release and Flaming Gorge package, public announcement), not just the final release figure.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading confirmed the exact release-reduction wording: OFF-023 states Interior 'implemented an action under Section 6.E of the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS ROD by reducing Lake Powell's annual release from 7.48 maf to 6.00 maf in WY 2026'; OFF-035 states Reclamation intends to release '660,000 acre-feet to 1 maf from Flaming Gorge Reservoir from April 2026 through April 2027' under the 2019 Drought Response Operating Agreements. Both figures are confirmed as stated, not paraphrased.

items.title: Tributary sediment monitoring translates into an HFE release decision
items.operational_question: How does tributary sediment input, monitored and modeled as a sand-mass balance, translate into a High-Flow Experiment (HFE) release decision at Glen Canyon Dam, and what can override an otherwise-triggered release?
items.synthesis_claim: Since 2012, Paria River tributary sand inputs are tracked and used to run a fall sand-mass-balance accounting process (July 1-November 30) that determines HFE eligibility; the formal 2012 protocol and 2016 LTEMP ROD translate that sediment signal into a release of up to ~45,000 cfs combining full powerplant and bypass-tube capacity, but the same ROD lets the legal requirement to meet the annual release volume override an otherwise-eligible extended-duration HFE, and post-release monitoring feeds back into the program's understanding of protocol effectiveness.
items.scope_and_conditions: Applies to Glen Canyon Dam HFEs conducted under the post-2012 protocol and the 2016 LTEMP ROD (Alternative D); does not apply to the pre-2012 experimental flows discussed in SC-LP-013.

analysis_chain.statement: Paria River tributary sand inputs are monitored and modeled as the sand-mass-balance basis for HFE eligibility, with a 10-year protocol implementing one to two HFEs annually timed to follow fall and/or spring sand inputs.

The 2012 DOI-approved protocol coordinates dam releases to follow large tributary sand inputs; under LTEMP Alternative D, extended-duration (greater than 96-hour) fall HFEs are capped at no more than four occurrences over the 20-year LTEMP period, triggered by the modeled sand-mass balance for the July 1-November 30 accounting period.

An extended-duration HFE will not be implemented if doing so would affect the annual release volume, meaning the legal requirement to meet that year's annual release volume can override an otherwise sediment-triggered extended-duration HFE.

An HFE release is defined as using full powerplant capacity (about 30,000 cfs) plus the four river-outlet-works bypass tubes (about 15,000 cfs), for a combined magnitude up to about 45,000 cfs, with durations of about 2-7 days (most standard HFEs capped at 96 hours).

The 45-site long-term sandbar monitoring network, together with daily repeat photography and annual surveys for 2012-2018 HFEs, measures post-HFE sandbar response, informing the program's evolving understanding of protocol effectiveness.

supporting_evidence.summary: High-flow experiments (HFEs) — short-duration controlled floods released from Glen Canyon Dam to rebuild sandbars — are conducted under a decision-making protocol approved by the Department of the Interior in 2012 that coordinates dam releases to occur following large sand inputs delivered to the Colorado River by a major tributary.

supporting_evidence.summary: High flow experiments were tested in 1996, 1997, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2013, and 2014 to rebuild eroded sandbars; since 2012 a 10-year protocol implements one to two high flow experiments annually, timed to follow tributary sand inputs from the Paria River in fall and/or spring.

supporting_evidence.summary: Under Alternative D's updated High-Flow Experiment (HFE) protocol, spring and fall HFE releases (1 to 250 hours long, 31,500 to 45,000 cfs) are triggered by the modeled sand mass balance from Paria River sediment inputs during defined spring (Dec 1-Jun 30) and fall (Jul 1-Nov 30) accounting periods, and extended-duration fall HFEs (>96 hr) are capped at four occurrences over the 20-year LTEMP period.

supporting_evidence.summary: Extended-duration fall HFEs will not be implemented if doing so would affect the annual release volume, meaning water-delivery constraints can override an otherwise-triggered extended HFE test.

supporting_evidence.summary: High-flow experimental releases (HFEs) between approximately 30,000 and 45,000 cfs are triggered when there is sufficient sediment input from the Paria River, and are used to mobilize sand stored in the river channel and redeposit it as sandbars, beaches, and associated backwater/riparian habitat downstream of Glen Canyon Dam.

supporting_evidence.summary: The sandbar monitoring dataset comprises ~1,800 repeat topographic/bathymetric surveys made annually or more frequently at 45 long-term study sites, which together represent only 7 to 9 percent of all sandbars in Marble and Grand Canyons respectively, yet were shown by comparison with larger samples to provide a consistent characterization of average sandbar response system-wide.

supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Discussion, Sandbar Response to the High-Flow Experiment Protocol section

supporting_evidence.summary: High flow experiments were tested in 1996, 1997, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2013, and 2014 to rebuild eroded sandbars; since 2012 a 10-year protocol implements one to two high flow experiments annually, timed to follow tributary sand inputs from the Paria River in fall and/or spring (EU-LP-RES-014-05). This decision-making protocol, approved by the Department of the Interior in 2012, coordinates dam releases to occur following large sand inputs delivered to the Colorado River by a major tributary (EU-LP-RES-018-01). Across the full historical record, 11 HFEs were released from Glen Canyon Dam between 1996 and November 2018, with peak magnitudes ranging from 864 to 1,274 cubic meters per second and durations from 24 to 168 hours, including lower-magnitude habitat maintenance flows (HMFs) in 1997 and 2000 (EU-LP-RES-018-02).

High-Flow Experiment (HFE) releases from Glen Canyon Dam are triggered when there is sufficient sediment input from the Paria River and typically range from approximately 30,000 to 45,000 cfs, used to mobilize channel-stored sand and redeposit it as sandbars, beaches, and associated backwater/riparian habitat. An HFE is defined as using full powerplant capacity (30,000 cfs) plus the four bypass (river outlet) tubes (15,000 cfs), for a combined magnitude up to about 45,000 cfs depending on the number of functional generators/penstocks, with release durations of about 2 to 7 days. Most HFEs are limited to a maximum duration of 96 hours under the 2011 HFE protocol, though some LTEMP alternatives allow extended-duration HFEs when adequate sediment supply is available.

Under LTEMP Alternative D, extended-duration fall HFEs (greater than 96 hours) are capped at no more than four occurrences over the 20-year LTEMP period, triggered by the modeled sand mass balance from Paria River sediment inputs during the defined fall accounting period (July 1-November 30). However, an extended-duration HFE will not be implemented if doing so would affect the annual release volume -- meaning the legal requirement to meet the annual release volume can override an otherwise-triggered extended-duration fall HFE.

Glen Canyon Dam's High-Flow Experiment (HFE) protocol effectiveness is tracked through a network of 45 long-term sandbar monitoring sites, part of a larger repeat topographic/bathymetric survey program (approximately 1,800 surveys) that represents only 7-9 percent of all sandbars in Marble and Grand Canyons but has been shown, by comparison with larger samples, to consistently characterize system-wide average sandbar response. At these 45 sites, sandbars were measured as larger at 52%, 52%, and 57% of sites immediately following the 2012, 2013, and 2014 HFEs respectively, with total sand volume at these sites increasing over the program's first 4 years. For the five HFEs released between 2012 and 2018, pre/post-event topographic surveys were not conducted; instead sandbar response was assessed via daily repeat photographs from remote automated cameras plus annual monitoring surveys collected approximately 11 months after each event.

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The frequency cap and its volume-protection override are both drawn from a single source (2016 LTEMP ROD Attachment B, Section 2.1.4); no independent second source in this corpus corroborates the specific 'four occurrences over 20 years' figure, so it should be treated as ROD-stated but not cross-source confirmed.
items.operational_implication: A user asking why a longer HFE was not run in a given year needs to see both the sediment-trigger logic and the annual-volume override, since either one alone could explain a non-implemented extended HFE.

items.title: Physical, elevation-graded, and reliability constraints jointly define release capacity below minimum power pool
items.operational_question: As Lake Powell's elevation declines toward and below minimum power pool (3,490 ft), what jointly binding physical, elevation-graded, and reliability constraints define the feasible Glen Canyon Dam release volume, and how much flexibility remains?
items.synthesis_claim: Below elevation 3,490 ft, Glen Canyon Dam's release path narrows from eight penstocks to only the river outlet works (ROW), whose own per-tube capacity is further reduced by cavitation limits as elevation falls; Reclamation's own 2024 assessment additionally concludes the ROW cannot be reliably used as a sole long-term release path, while the Law of the River's 8.23 maf/year minimum objective release remains legally in force regardless of this shrinking physical capacity -- together defining why Reclamation treats 3,490 ft (and the 3,525 ft DROA buffer above it) as hard operating priorities rather than discretionary targets.
items.scope_and_conditions: Applies to Glen Canyon Dam operations as Lake Powell elevation approaches or falls below 3,490 ft (minimum power pool); figures reflect 2024 interim operating guidance and pre-existing design documentation.

analysis_chain.statement: Above 3,490 ft, releases pass through eight penstocks; below 3,490 ft the powerplant cannot be used at all, leaving only the four river-outlet-works tubes, physically limited to about 15,000 cfs total at unrestricted design capacity.

ROW per-tube capacity is itself cavitation-limited and steps down further as elevation drops, from about 3,185 cfs per tube at 3,490 ft to 2,200 cfs at 3,420 ft, 1,200 cfs at 3,400 ft, and 0 cfs at 3,390 ft under the 2024 interim operating guidance.

Reclamation's 2024 Technical Decision Memorandum concludes the ROW were never designed for sustained long-term conveyance, documenting a 1965 tailrace failure and 2023 cavitation damage as evidence the ROW should not be relied upon as the sole release path.

The Law of the River's 8.23 maf/year minimum objective release remains in force regardless of physical capacity; a low-elevation, ROW-limited scenario (e.g., only 7.41 maf/year available at elevation 3,430 ft) would fall well short of this obligation.

The institutional response is to operate to keep Lake Powell at or above 3,490 ft (and ideally above the 3,525 ft DROA buffer) rather than test a sustained ROW-only regime, since dead pool at 3,370 ft would leave no controlled release path at all.

supporting_evidence.summary: The River Outlet Works have historically only been opened when the dam was first filled, during short-term high-flow experiments, and for emergency flood releases in the early 1980s, and have never been used over extended periods.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Regulation of Colorado River Flows section, footnote 18

supporting_evidence.summary: Below minimum power pool, the only remaining way to pass water through Glen Canyon Dam is the river outlet works (bypass tubes): two intakes leading to four 96-inch-diameter steel pipes with a combined maximum discharge capacity of 15,000 cubic feet per second.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; main article body

supporting_evidence.summary: Glen Canyon Dam's combined spillway discharge capacity is 208,000 cfs at elevation 3,700.0 ft (via two spillway tunnels, each with two 40- by 52.5-foot radial gates), and the combined river outlet works capacity is 15,000 cfs, providing the dam's flood-release and emergency discharge capability.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; project description / Hydraulics & Hydrology fields

supporting_evidence.summary: To limit cavitation risk in the river outlet works at low reservoir levels, Reclamation set interim maximum per-conduit flow limits below the 3,750 cfs design maximum, stepping down with elevation - e.g., 3,185 cfs at elevation 3,490 ft, 2,200 cfs at 3,420 ft, 1,200 cfs at 3,400 ft, and 0 cfs at 3,390 ft.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Section A Purpose, guidance item 2 and Table 1

supporting_evidence.summary: The river outlet works, consisting of four 96-inch-diameter steel pipes near the left abutment, were designed with a capacity of 15,000 cfs at reservoir elevation 3,490 feet (minimum power-operation water surface), providing releases when the powerplant is not operating and during final closure of the diversion tunnels.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; River Outlets section

supporting_evidence.summary: Below a Lake Powell elevation of 3,550 feet, Glen Canyon Dam's river outlet works have reduced release capacity; SEIS modeling assumed each of the four outlet tubes is limited to 3,150 cfs (12,600 cfs total) rather than the unrestricted maximum of 3,750 cfs per tube (15,000 cfs total).
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Chapter 1.9 Operational Considerations

supporting_evidence.summary: Original Glen Canyon Dam design references indicate the river outlet works were never intended for long-term water conveyance at low reservoir levels; historically they were used only to augment powerplant/spillway discharges for short durations (e.g., 1983 flood releases about three months, high-flow experiments lasting days to a week).
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Section D.2 Dependence on Long-Term Operation of River Outlet Works

supporting_evidence.summary: A 2023 special inspection of the Glen Canyon Dam river outlet works found the hollow-jet valves, pipes, and ring-follower gates sufficient for periodic/seasonal releases, but flagged concern about using the outlet works for long-term high-flow releases and recommended a major overhaul or replacement for high confidence in continuous long-term operation.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Section D.4 Reliability of Hollow-Jet Valve Operations

supporting_evidence.summary: On April 20, 1965, while the reservoir was at elevation 3,490 ft with four of eight powerplant units operating and outlets variably open, the Glen Canyon Dam tailrace stabilization slab was undermined by a recirculating eddy from river outlet works operation and portions of it collapsed, because tailwater was 4-6 feet lower than predicted by physical modeling.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Section D.5 Tailrace Scour and Sediment Deposition

supporting_evidence.summary: Reclamation's formal conclusion is that it should not rely on the river outlet works as the sole means for releasing water from Glen Canyon Dam, as would be required at reservoir levels below the minimum power pool elevation of 3,490 ft, given current uncertainty about long-term conduit and hollow-jet valve performance and tailrace sedimentation.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Section E Conclusions

supporting_evidence.summary: In 2023, when the river outlet works were used to conduct a high-flow release into the Grand Canyon at low-reservoir levels, damaging cavitation occurred, and the Bureau has warned that further extended use would likely cause more.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; main article body

supporting_evidence.summary: Reclamation's original Technical Record of Design and Construction established elevation 3,490 ft as the minimum reservoir elevation for power production, 20 ft above the penstock intake centerline (elevation 3,470 ft); water cannot be released through the penstocks below 3,490 ft (OFF-025-03). Multiple later sources restate this same threshold: Reclamation estimates the depth for minimum power pool is 20 ft above the penstocks, i.e. elevation 3,490 fasl (CRS-002-02); at 3,490 ft, minimum power pool is 20 ft above the generators' actual penstock intakes, and the dam's eight turbines must be shut down at minimum power pool to avoid cavitation (MED-002-01); the 1999 multi-level intake structure hydraulic model study likewise designates elevation 3,490 ft as the minimum water surface for power operations (OFF-028-06); the 2016 LTEMP Final EIS states hydropower production would cease if Lake Powell drops below approximately 3,490 ft (OFF-005-01); the 2024 Near-term Operations SEIS ROD notes dry hydrology in recent years produced low Lake Powell elevations at levels such as 3,490 ft, giving Reclamation operating experience at this threshold (OFF-002-06); the 2024 LTEMP Final Supplemental EIS states Reclamation's Interim Operating Guidance for Low Reservoir Levels directs use of the full extent of Upper Colorado Basin operational capabilities to try to keep Lake Powell at or above elevation 3,490 ft (OFF-007-03); and an April 2026 status report reiterates that hydropower generation stops at 3,490 feet, with the reservoir at 3,526 feet at that time and Reclamation aiming to keep it above 3,500 feet (MED-001-04).

Glen Canyon Dam's design-basis minimum water surface elevation for power operation is 3,490 feet, with the eight penstock intakes centered at elevation 3,470 feet (about 45 feet above the estimated silt elevation projected after 150 years of reservoir operation). Reflecting this design threshold, Reclamation's March 2024 interim operating guidance directs exercising the full extent of Upper Colorado Basin operational capabilities to attempt to maintain Lake Powell at or above elevation 3,490 ft, so as to preserve redundant downstream delivery through both the penstocks and the river outlet works.

The river outlet works (four 96-inch-diameter steel pipes) were designed with an unrestricted capacity of 3,750 cfs per tube (15,000 cfs total) at reservoir elevation 3,490 ft (minimum power-operation water surface). Below elevation 3,550 ft, however, the 2024 LTEMP Final SEIS's modeling assumed a reduced capacity of 3,150 cfs per tube (12,600 cfs total) rather than the unrestricted 3,750 cfs/tube maximum. Separately, Reclamation's March 2024 interim operating guidance set even more granular, elevation-stepped interim maximum per-conduit flow limits to limit cavitation risk, including 3,185 cfs at elevation 3,490 ft, stepping down to 2,200 cfs at 3,420 ft, 1,200 cfs at 3,400 ft, and 0 cfs at 3,390 ft.

When Lake Powell drops below the minimum power pool elevation of 3,490 feet, Glen Canyon Dam can no longer release water through its powerplant turbines/penstocks and must rely on the river outlet works (ROW), whose capacity is limited and increases with pool elevation (OFF-021-08); the Post-2026 Draft EIS states the dam 'was not envisioned to operate below minimum power pool (elevation 3,490 feet)' and that below this elevation water must be released through the jet tubes at the end of the ROW instead of the penstocks (OFF-019-05). Across all anticipated post-2026 operating alternatives, releases from Lake Powell may fall below the alternative's specified release volume at elevations below 3,490 feet due to this infrastructure limitation (OFF-020-04). A separate study quantified the resulting shortfall: at elevation 3,430 feet, the ROW can discharge only 10,200 cfs (7.41 MAF/year), considerably less than the Law of the River's 8.23 MAF/year delivery requirement, and below the ROW's own elevation of 3,370 feet, approximately 1.89 MAF becomes inaccessible dead storage (CRS-002-08).

Multiple sources indicate the river outlet works (ROW) were not designed for, and cannot be fully relied upon for, long-term or high-flow releases at low Lake Powell levels. Reclamation's 2024 Technical Decision Memorandum found no design reference indicating the ROW were intended for long-term water conveyance at low reservoir levels; historically they were used only to augment powerplant/spillway discharges for short durations (e.g., about three months during 1983 flood releases, days to a week for high-flow experiments) (OFF-025-04). A 2023 special inspection found the hollow-jet valves, pipes, and ring-follower gates sufficient for periodic/seasonal releases but flagged concern about long-term high-flow use and recommended a major overhaul or replacement for high confidence in continuous long-term operation (OFF-025-05). This concern has historical precedent: on April 20, 1965, at reservoir elevation 3,490 ft with the ROW variably open, the dam's tailrace stabilization slab was undermined by a recirculating eddy from ROW operation and portions of it collapsed, because tailwater was 4-6 feet lower than had been predicted by physical modeling (OFF-025-06). More recently, in 2023, when the ROW were used for a high-flow release into the Grand Canyon at low-reservoir levels, damaging cavitation occurred, and the Bureau has warned further extended use would likely cause more (MED-002-03). Based on this evidence, Reclamation's formal conclusion is that it should not rely on the ROW as the sole means of releasing water from Glen Canyon Dam, as would be required below minimum power pool (3,490 ft), given current uncertainty about long-term conduit and hollow-jet valve performance and tailrace sedimentation (OFF-025-07).

The 2016 LTEMP Final EIS states Glen Canyon Dam is designed to operate between the outlet works intake elevation of 3,370 ft AMSL and the top of the live storage pool at 3,700 ft AMSL (OFF-005-01). High Country News reporting states that if Lake Powell drops to the river outlet works' (ROW) elevation of 3,370 feet, the reservoir reaches "dead pool," where water passes through the dam only when river flow exceeds evaporation losses, with no lower intakes or spillways available (MED-002-04). The 2018 USGS resurvey, using the NAVD88 vertical datum, places the dead storage elevation (below all hydroelectric penstocks and other outlet works) at 3,372.91 ft NAVD88 (RES-013-04).

Under the Upper Basin DCP's DROA, Upper Basin states agreed to operate system units to keep Lake Powell's surface above elevation 3,525 feet, 35 feet above minimum power pool (EU-LP-CRS-001-04). Reclamation's stated operational goal under DROA is to 'protect' this 3,525-ft elevation, primarily via reduced Glen Canyon Dam releases and drawdown of upstream initial-unit reservoirs (EU-LP-CRS-002-04). The DROA establishes the process for Reclamation, in collaboration with the Upper Basin States, to release additional water from upstream CRSP initial-unit reservoirs (Flaming Gorge, Aspinall, Navajo, Glen Canyon/Lake Powell) to reduce the risk of Lake Powell reaching critical elevation (EU-LP-OFF-017-03). In CRSS modeling, Powell Infrastructure Protection (PIP) releases from the Upper Initial Units (Flaming Gorge, Blue Mesa, Navajo) are specifically triggered when Lake Powell is projected to fall below elevation 3,525 feet (EU-LP-OFF-021-06). This target was actually invoked when the July 2025 24-Month Study projected Lake Powell declining below the 3,525.00-ft DROA target elevation, triggering DROA year-2025 drought-response planning under the DCP-related agreements (EU-LP-OFF-022-03); consistent with protecting this same target, the December 2025 24-Month Study reduced Glen Canyon Dam's monthly release volumes for December 2025 through April 2026 by 0.598 maf (EU-LP-OFF-023-03).

items.uncertainty_or_exception: Full powerplant/penstock capacity is itself contested elsewhere in this corpus (31,500 vs. approximately 33,000-33,200 cfs, KC-LP-OPR-15), and ROW per-tube capacity figures differ slightly across sources (3,150 vs. 3,185 cfs at similar elevations, KC-LP-OPR-07); neither discrepancy changes the qualitative constraint structure but both should be flagged before citing an exact cfs figure. The 3,370 ft vs. 3,372.91 ft dead-pool figure reflects a NAVD88 vertical-datum/rounding difference, not a substantive conflict.
items.operational_implication: This constraint structure is the physical basis for the emergency drought-response actions analyzed in SC-LP-001 and SC-LP-009; a report or index should link the physical-capacity constraint directly to those decision/regime-change cards rather than presenting them independently.

items.title: Safety, sediment, and power-flexibility constraints jointly define the MLFF/LTEMP hourly-release envelope
items.operational_question: What jointly relevant safety/recreation, sediment/ecosystem, and power-system-flexibility constraints define Glen Canyon Dam's allowable hourly and daily release pattern under MLFF and LTEMP Alternative D?
items.synthesis_claim: The 1996 ROD set a baseline safety/recreation-driven envelope (minimum/maximum release, ramp rates, and a 3-tier daily-fluctuation cap) grounded in a 1995 river-guide/public preference study; the 2016 LTEMP ROD then revised the fluctuation formula and down-ramp rate specifically to reduce sandbar erosion, while WAPA continues to exercise discretionary hourly/weekly dispatch choices inside these limits that it can alter without a new NEPA/ROD process, leaving the up-ramp rate the one figure unchanged since 1996.
items.scope_and_conditions: Applies to Glen Canyon Dam's sub-annual (hourly/daily/monthly) release pattern under MLFF (1996-2016) and LTEMP Alternative D (2016-present); does not govern total annual release volume (see KC-LP-REG-05 / SC-LP-006).

analysis_chain.statement: The 1996 ROD set a minimum release of 8,000 cfs (day) / 5,000 cfs (night), a maximum release of 25,000 cfs, an up-ramp limit of 4,000 cfs/hour, a down-ramp limit of 1,500 cfs/hour, and a 3-tier daily-fluctuation cap topping out at 8,000 cfs/day, based on a 1995 study of river-guide and public flow preferences.

LTEMP Alternative D (2016 ROD) replaced the fixed 3-tier fluctuation schedule with a formula proportional to that month's release volume (9-10x monthly volume in kaf) and raised the down-ramp limit to 2,500 cfs/hour, changes explicitly framed as reducing sandbar erosion rates.

analysis_chain.stage: power-flexibility constraint operating within the above
analysis_chain.statement: WAPA's discretionary hourly and weekly dispatch practice -- maximizing releases during peak-demand periods (Monday-Saturday, 7 a.m.-11 p.m.) and keeping weekend releases at no less than 85 percent of average weekday release -- operates inside these formal limits and can be altered by WAPA at any time without a new ROD/EIS process.

Since the 1991 interim criteria preceded the 1996 ROD, the maximum release and down-ramp limits have been loosened twice (1991 to 1996, then 1996 to 2016) to restore power-production flexibility, while the up-ramp rate (4,000 cfs/hour) and the 8,000 cfs/day fluctuation ceiling have remained the two constants across both revisions.

supporting_evidence.summary: Since the 1996 Record of Decision selected the Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) alternative (codified in the 1997 Operating Criteria), Glen Canyon Dam releases have been bound by a consistent set of limits, repeated across CRS reports, LTEMP EIS chapters, biological opinions/assessments, GAO review, and peer-reviewed research: minimum release of 8,000 cfs from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. and 5,000 cfs at night; maximum release of 25,000 cfs (well below the approximately 31,500 cfs turbine/penstock capacity, i.e. about 76% of unrestricted capacity at elevation 3,700 ft); ascending (up) ramp rate up to 4,000 cfs/hour; descending (down) ramp rate up to 1,500 cfs/hour; and an allowable daily flow fluctuation that scales with that month's total release volume -- 5,000 cfs/day for monthly release volumes under 0.6 maf (600 kaf), 6,000 cfs/day for 0.6-0.8 maf (600-800 kaf), and 8,000 cfs/day for volumes over 0.8 maf (800 kaf). A peer-reviewed research paper (RES-018) restates the same limits in metric units (141 m3/s minimum, 708 m3/s maximum, and 142/170/227 m3/s daily fluctuation tiers), confirming unit-equivalence with the cfs figures used elsewhere.

The 8,000 cfs maximum daily fluctuation limit (the top tier of the MLFF sliding-scale fluctuation rule) was established in the 1996 Record of Decision to address safety, recreation, and sediment concerns, based on a 1995 study (Reclamation 1995) of river-guide/public flow preferences. Under the LTEMP Final EIS (2016), this same 8,000 cfs cap is retained and is present in both the No Action Alternative and the LTEMP preferred alternative (Alternative D).

Under LTEMP Alternative D (the 2016 ROD selected alternative), the allowable within-day fluctuation range is no longer a fixed 3-tier schedule but a formula proportional to that month's scheduled release volume: 10 x monthly volume (kaf) in June-August, and 9 x monthly volume (kaf) in other months, subject to an overall cap (stated elsewhere as 227 m3/s, approximately 8,000 cfs). Alternative D also raises the down-ramp (descending) rate limit to no more than 2,500 cfs/hour (1,000 cfs/hour greater than the prior No-Action/MLFF limit of 1,500 cfs/hour), while retaining the up-ramp (ascending) rate at 4,000 cfs/hour, unchanged from MLFF. A companion research paper restates these LTEMP ramp rates in metric units: 113 m3/s/hour increasing (~4,000 cfs/hr) and 71 m3/s/hour decreasing (~2,500 cfs/hr), explicitly framed as a change made to reduce sandbar erosion rates.

Beyond formal ROD requirements, WAPA follows discretionary dispatch practices at Glen Canyon Dam -- such as holding nightly generation to the same minimum level during off-peak hours and keeping weekend releases at no less than 85 percent of the average weekday release -- that fall within MLFF constraints but are not ROD requirements and can be altered or abandoned by WAPA at any time (EU-LP-OFF-005-10). Per the 1997 GAO report, to the extent possible Glen Canyon Dam's hourly power operations followed three guidelines: maximize water releases during peak energy demand periods (generally Monday-Saturday, 7 a.m. to 11 p.m.); maximize releases during peak-demand months and minimize during low-demand months; and minimize or eliminate powerplant bypasses (EU-LP-OFF-010-13).

Beginning November 1, 1991, Reclamation implemented interim operating criteria for Glen Canyon Dam that cut the approved maximum peak release from 31,500 cfs to 20,000 cfs, restricted daily fluctuations to a range of 5,000-8,000 cfs, and capped ramp rates at 2,500 cfs/hour increasing and 1,500 cfs/hour decreasing, while still meeting the 8.23 maf minimum annual release. Between the draft and final EIS that led to the 1996 Record of Decision, these same starting values were revised: the up-ramp rate limit was increased from 2,500 to 4,000 cfs/hour, and the maximum allowable release was increased from 20,000 to 25,000 cfs, specifically to enhance power production flexibility in response to public comments.

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The EU set does not state whether the volume-proportional Alternative D fluctuation formula can ever exceed the legacy 8,000 cfs/day cap in very high-release months; this card treats the cap as still binding per the 'subject to an overall cap' language in KC-LP-OPR-03, but the exact interaction with high-volume equalization years was not independently verified against the original ROD text here.
items.operational_implication: Distinguishes 'hard' ROD-level limits that require a NEPA/ROD process to change from WAPA's day-to-day discretionary dispatch choices that can shift without formal process -- relevant to any question about whether Glen Canyon Dam could operate differently tomorrow versus only after rulemaking.

items.title: MLFF/LTEMP ramp-rate limits trade hydropower flexibility against downstream ecosystem protection
items.operational_question: How does the MLFF/LTEMP ramp-rate and fluctuation regime trade power-generation flexibility against downstream ecosystem and sediment protection, and what is the quantified cost of that tradeoff?
items.synthesis_claim: The 1996 ROD selected MLFF specifically to reduce daily flow fluctuations well below historic peaking levels in order to protect downstream sediment, fish, and recreation resources; this benefit to the ecosystem objective came at a documented, quantified cost to the power objective, reducing WAPA's operating flexibility and costing WAPA and its customers an average of $38-50 million per year between 1997 and 2005, while the LTEMP framework's Grand Canyon Protection Act mandate leaves total annual release volume (and the bulk of associated hydropower revenue) outside its scope.
items.scope_and_conditions: Applies to the ramp-rate and daily-fluctuation restrictions in force since the 1996 ROD, with the $38-50 million/year cost figure specific to the 1997-2005 period under the original MLFF tiers, prior to LTEMP Alternative D's 2016 revisions.

analysis_chain.statement: The 1996 ROD selected the Modified Low Fluctuating Flow alternative specifically to reduce daily flow fluctuations well below historic peaking levels, in order to protect or enhance downstream resources while allowing limited power-operation flexibility.

LTEMP Alternative D's ramp-rate revisions (a lower fixed down-ramp change and a volume-proportional fluctuation formula) are explicitly framed as reducing sandbar erosion rates relative to the prior MLFF schedule.

This same restriction reduced WAPA's operating flexibility, prompting WAPA to modify commitments made to its power customers, and cost WAPA and its customers an average of $38-50 million per year between 1997 and 2005 because ramping restrictions prevented hourly generation adjustment to match power demand.

LTEMP's purpose statement frames it as adaptively managing operations consistent with the Grand Canyon Protection Act, subordinating power flexibility to downstream-resource protection within its 20-year scope, while explicitly leaving total annual release volume -- and thus most hydropower revenue -- outside LTEMP's scope.

supporting_evidence.summary: In the 1996 Record of Decision, the Secretary selected the Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) Alternative as Glen Canyon Dam's operating criteria, explicitly because it would reduce daily flow fluctuations well below the 'no action' (historic peaking) levels of releases while providing high steady releases of short duration to protect or enhance downstream resources, allowing limited flexibility for power operations. A peer-reviewed research paper confirms MLFF became the dam's operating regime in 1996, replacing hydroelectric peaking operations, and was the preferred alternative identified in the 1995 Environmental Impact Statement as an adaptive strategy for improving downstream Colorado River ecosystem resources.

The LTEMP's stated purpose is to provide a comprehensive framework for adaptively managing Glen Canyon Dam operations over a 20-year period, consistent with the Grand Canyon Protection Act (GCPA) and other applicable federal law. This purpose statement is repeated in near-identical language in both the 2016 LTEMP Record of Decision and the LTEMP Final EIS Chapter 1, and is independently corroborated by a 2021 Reclamation SECURE Water Act report to Congress describing LTEMP (finalized via EIS in October 2016) as establishing a 20-year adaptive management framework consistent with the GCPA.

The 1996 ROD's Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) operating criteria reduced Glen Canyon Dam powerplant's operating flexibility and, consequently, its economic value. An ex post economic analysis found this reduction in flexibility prompted the Western Area Power Administration (WAPA) to modify commitments made to its customers (RES-026-01). A separate LTEMP EIS accounting found that between 1997 and 2005, this operational restriction cost WAPA and its power customers an average of $38 million to $50 million per year, since MLFF ramping restrictions prevented generation from adjusting hourly to match power demand, forcing increased reliance on alternate generating resources (OFF-005-08).

Since the 1996 Record of Decision selected the Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) alternative (codified in the 1997 Operating Criteria), Glen Canyon Dam releases have been bound by a consistent set of limits, repeated across CRS reports, LTEMP EIS chapters, biological opinions/assessments, GAO review, and peer-reviewed research: minimum release of 8,000 cfs from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. and 5,000 cfs at night; maximum release of 25,000 cfs (well below the approximately 31,500 cfs turbine/penstock capacity, i.e. about 76% of unrestricted capacity at elevation 3,700 ft); ascending (up) ramp rate up to 4,000 cfs/hour; descending (down) ramp rate up to 1,500 cfs/hour; and an allowable daily flow fluctuation that scales with that month's total release volume -- 5,000 cfs/day for monthly release volumes under 0.6 maf (600 kaf), 6,000 cfs/day for 0.6-0.8 maf (600-800 kaf), and 8,000 cfs/day for volumes over 0.8 maf (800 kaf). A peer-reviewed research paper (RES-018) restates the same limits in metric units (141 m3/s minimum, 708 m3/s maximum, and 142/170/227 m3/s daily fluctuation tiers), confirming unit-equivalence with the cfs figures used elsewhere.

Under LTEMP Alternative D (the 2016 ROD selected alternative), the allowable within-day fluctuation range is no longer a fixed 3-tier schedule but a formula proportional to that month's scheduled release volume: 10 x monthly volume (kaf) in June-August, and 9 x monthly volume (kaf) in other months, subject to an overall cap (stated elsewhere as 227 m3/s, approximately 8,000 cfs). Alternative D also raises the down-ramp (descending) rate limit to no more than 2,500 cfs/hour (1,000 cfs/hour greater than the prior No-Action/MLFF limit of 1,500 cfs/hour), while retaining the up-ramp (ascending) rate at 4,000 cfs/hour, unchanged from MLFF. A companion research paper restates these LTEMP ramp rates in metric units: 113 m3/s/hour increasing (~4,000 cfs/hr) and 71 m3/s/hour decreasing (~2,500 cfs/hr), explicitly framed as a change made to reduce sandbar erosion rates.

The LTEMP (including its 2016 ROD and 2024 SEIS amendment) governs only the monthly, daily, and hourly release pattern from Glen Canyon Dam. It does not control the total annual release volume, which remains governed separately by the Long-Range Operating Criteria (LROC) as currently implemented through the 2007 Interim Guidelines (and, for the 2024 amendment, as further supplemented by the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS). Because of this scope boundary, LTEMP does not modify determinations made under the Interim Shortage Guidelines for Lake Powell and Lake Mead and does not trigger an off-cycle mid-year review of reservoir operations.

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The $38-50 million/year figure covers only 1997-2005 and derives from a single LTEMP EIS citation of Veselka et al. 2010; no more recent (post-2016, Alternative D) recomputation of this cost exists in this EU set, so the tradeoff's current-dollar magnitude is dated and likely does not reflect Alternative D's loosened down-ramp and fluctuation formula.
items.operational_implication: Any economic argument for loosening MLFF/LTEMP constraints further should be benchmarked against this same historical $38-50 million/year estimate, and any environmental argument for tightening them should note that the annual-volume/hydropower-revenue base itself is legally untouched by LTEMP.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading confirmed the dollar figure verbatim: OFF-005 states 'since the implementation of MLFF, between 1997 and 2005, the average annual cost incurred ranged from $38 million to $50 million, due to operational restrictions (Veselka et al. 2010).' RES-026's abstract independently corroborates the institutional response: the ROD restrictions 'reduced the operating flexibility of the hydroelectric power plant and therefore its economic value,' prompting WAPA 'to modify commitments that it made to its customers.'

items.title: Extended-duration HFE sediment benefit is subordinate to the legal annual-release-volume obligation
items.operational_question: How does the extended-duration HFE frequency rule trade sediment-rebuilding benefits against the legal requirement to meet the annual release volume?
items.synthesis_claim: Extended-duration fall HFEs are designed to maximize sediment redistribution when tributary sand supply is high, but the 2016 LTEMP ROD explicitly subordinates this ecological opportunity to the legal annual-release-volume obligation: an eligible extended-duration HFE will not be implemented if doing so would affect that year's annual release volume, meaning the delivery obligation automatically wins whenever the two objectives conflict.
items.scope_and_conditions: Applies specifically to extended-duration (greater than 96-hour) fall HFEs under LTEMP Alternative D; standard-duration HFEs and the underlying annual release volume itself are governed separately from LTEMP (see KC-LP-REG-05).

analysis_chain.statement: Extended-duration fall HFEs (greater than 96 hours, up to four occurrences over the 20-year LTEMP period) are designed to maximize sediment redistribution to rebuild sandbars and habitat when Paria River sediment supply is high.

analysis_chain.stage: legal constraint on the same resource
analysis_chain.statement: The annual release-volume requirement (e.g., the LROC's 8.23 maf minimum objective, or whichever tier volume governs that year) sits entirely outside LTEMP's scope and is not something an HFE decision is permitted to alter.

The 2016 LTEMP ROD states an extended-duration HFE will not be implemented if doing so would affect the annual release volume, meaning the legal delivery obligation overrides an otherwise sediment-triggered extended-duration HFE.

An eligible sediment/tributary-sand trigger in a given year does not guarantee an extended HFE will occur, because a downstream water-delivery/volume conflict can override it even when the sediment mass-balance condition is met.

supporting_evidence.summary: Under Alternative D's updated High-Flow Experiment (HFE) protocol, spring and fall HFE releases (1 to 250 hours long, 31,500 to 45,000 cfs) are triggered by the modeled sand mass balance from Paria River sediment inputs during defined spring (Dec 1-Jun 30) and fall (Jul 1-Nov 30) accounting periods, and extended-duration fall HFEs (>96 hr) are capped at four occurrences over the 20-year LTEMP period.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Attachment B Section 2.1 Sediment-Related Experiments / Section 2.1.4 Extended-Duration Fall HFEs

supporting_evidence.summary: High-flow experimental releases (HFEs) between approximately 30,000 and 45,000 cfs are triggered when there is sufficient sediment input from the Paria River, and are used to mobilize sand stored in the river channel and redeposit it as sandbars, beaches, and associated backwater/riparian habitat downstream of Glen Canyon Dam.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Section 1.2 Purpose of and Need for Action, key issues list

supporting_evidence.summary: The annual volume of water released from Glen Canyon Dam under the LTEMP is determined by the Long-Range Operating Criteria (LROC) as currently implemented through the 2007 Interim Guidelines until 2026; guidelines for annual releases after 2026 will be determined under a separate process under the terms of the 2007 Guidelines.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Section 1.5 Scope of the EIS

supporting_evidence.summary: Early Glen Canyon Dam operations followed the 1970 Criteria for Coordinated Long-Range Operation and the Filling Criteria for Lake Powell (terminated when the reservoir filled on June 22, 1980); the 1980-1987 period was controlled by the Long-Range Operating Criteria (LROC) focused on water delivery and power, and beginning in 1988 operations returned to the LROC-specified objective minimum release of 8.23 maf.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Section 3.2.1.1 Lake Powell Hydrology

supporting_evidence.summary: Extended-duration fall HFEs will not be implemented if doing so would affect the annual release volume, meaning water-delivery constraints can override an otherwise-triggered extended HFE test.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Attachment B Section 2.1.4 Extended-Duration Fall HFEs Under Alternative D

supporting_evidence.summary: Under LTEMP Alternative D, extended-duration fall HFEs (greater than 96 hours) are capped at no more than four occurrences over the 20-year LTEMP period, triggered by the modeled sand mass balance from Paria River sediment inputs during the defined fall accounting period (July 1-November 30). However, an extended-duration HFE will not be implemented if doing so would affect the annual release volume -- meaning the legal requirement to meet the annual release volume can override an otherwise-triggered extended-duration fall HFE.

High-Flow Experiment (HFE) releases from Glen Canyon Dam are triggered when there is sufficient sediment input from the Paria River and typically range from approximately 30,000 to 45,000 cfs, used to mobilize channel-stored sand and redeposit it as sandbars, beaches, and associated backwater/riparian habitat. An HFE is defined as using full powerplant capacity (30,000 cfs) plus the four bypass (river outlet) tubes (15,000 cfs), for a combined magnitude up to about 45,000 cfs depending on the number of functional generators/penstocks, with release durations of about 2 to 7 days. Most HFEs are limited to a maximum duration of 96 hours under the 2011 HFE protocol, though some LTEMP alternatives allow extended-duration HFEs when adequate sediment supply is available.

The LTEMP (including its 2016 ROD and 2024 SEIS amendment) governs only the monthly, daily, and hourly release pattern from Glen Canyon Dam. It does not control the total annual release volume, which remains governed separately by the Long-Range Operating Criteria (LROC) as currently implemented through the 2007 Interim Guidelines (and, for the 2024 amendment, as further supplemented by the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS). Because of this scope boundary, LTEMP does not modify determinations made under the Interim Shortage Guidelines for Lake Powell and Lake Mead and does not trigger an off-cycle mid-year review of reservoir operations.

The 1970 Criteria for Coordinated Long-Range Operation of Colorado River Reservoirs (LROC), Article II(2), establishes the objective of maintaining a minimum annual release from Lake Powell of 8.23 million acre-feet (maf). Reclamation returned to this objective minimum release beginning in 1988 after the 1980-1987 Long-Range Operating Criteria period. The 2007 Interim Guidelines, Section 6.C.1, likewise require a minimum of 8.23 maf to be released from Glen Canyon Dam each year, except for reductions specified by the Interim Guidelines. The 2008 Final Biological Opinion describes this 8.23 maf figure as Reclamation's baseline minimum objective annual release, with the proposed action allowing releases below it only under conditions defined in the Shortage Guidelines. As of the 2025 Post-2026 Alternatives Report, Reclamation affirms that under LROC Article II(2) the objective remains a minimum release of 8.23 maf, and plans to publish any annual deficits below that objective release alongside 10-year Lee Ferry aggregate flow metrics.

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The EU set does not document any specific historical year in which this override actually cancelled an eligible extended HFE; the tradeoff rule is confirmed as written policy but not yet confirmed as having produced an observed real-world cancellation.
items.operational_implication: Report language explaining why an extended HFE did not occur in a given year must check both the sediment trigger and this volume-protection override before concluding sediment supply alone was insufficient.

items.title: Warm-water releases benefiting humpback chub simultaneously raise nonnative-fish predation risk to the same species
items.operational_question: How does using warmer Glen Canyon Dam releases to benefit humpback chub simultaneously create nonnative-fish predation and competition risk to that same species, and what flow-based countermeasures has Reclamation used?
items.synthesis_claim: Reduced Lake Powell storage during drought warms Glen Canyon Dam releases in a way intended to benefit native humpback chub, but the same warming is modeled to also benefit nonnative fish, raising predation and competition pressure on humpback chub; Reclamation has responded with targeted suppression and management flows (2003-2005 fluctuating suppression releases, and Trout Management Flows under LTEMP Alternative D) and has institutionally committed to monitor and control nonnative fish if drought-driven warming recurs.
items.scope_and_conditions: Applies to Glen Canyon Dam release-temperature effects on humpback chub and nonnative fish (principally rainbow trout) under drought-driven low-storage conditions, as documented for the 2003-2011 and 2014 warming episodes and the LTEMP Alternative D management-flow tools.

analysis_chain.statement: River warming that occurred from 2003 to 2011 (and again in 2014), resulting from reduced Lake Powell storage, was intended to benefit native humpback chub reproduction and growth.

The Grand Canyon Ecosystem Model predicted that nonnative fish would also benefit from the same warming, potentially increasing predation and competition risk to humpback chub through greater fish interactions in critical river segments.

Reclamation implemented non-native fish suppression flows (daily fluctuations of 5,000-20,000 cfs, January-March 2003-2005) to limit non-native recruitment, and later Trout Management Flows under LTEMP Alternative D, triggered by predicted high rainbow trout recruitment at Lees Ferry.

The 2008 Final Biological Opinion ties this same warming-driven predation risk to prolonged drought (citing paleoclimate droughts of 15-20 years) and commits Reclamation to monitor and control nonnative fish through the Adaptive Management Program if such warming recurs.

supporting_evidence.summary: River warming from 2003 to 2011, resulting from reduced Lake Powell storage, was intended to benefit native humpback chub, but ecosystem modeling predicted that non-native fish would also benefit, potentially increasing predation and competition risk to humpback chub through greater fish interactions in critical river segments.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Experience of the Value of Ecosystem Modeling section

supporting_evidence.summary: As part of the 2002-2004 experimental program, Reclamation implemented non-native fish suppression releases from Glen Canyon Dam with daily fluctuations of 5,000-20,000 cfs during January 1-March 31 of 2003, and continued this high-fluctuation suppression flow pattern in 2004 and 2005 to test its effectiveness at limiting non-native fish recruitment.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Section 2.2.5 2002-2004 Experimental Releases from Glen Canyon Dam and Removal of Non-Native Fish

supporting_evidence.summary: Non-native fish suppression flows with daily fluctuations between 142 and 566 m3/s were released from Glen Canyon Dam each January through March from 2003 to 2005, representing a special-event departure from the standard MLFF/LTEMP flow regime implemented for a specific ecological management objective.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Flow Regimes and Tributary Sediment Supply section

supporting_evidence.summary: Trout Management Flows (TMFs) under Alternative D consist of repeated fluctuation cycles combining sustained high flows (e.g., 20,000 cfs) with a rapid drop to a very low flow (e.g., 5,000-8,000 cfs) intended to strand young-of-year trout; up to three TMF cycles per month may be tested over as many as four months (May-August).
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Attachment B Section 2.2.1 Trout Management Flows Under Alternative D

supporting_evidence.summary: Under the LTEMP preferred alternative (Alternative D), Trout Management Flows (TMFs) are triggered by the prediction of high recruitment of young-of-year rainbow trout at Lees Ferry, regardless of the cause of the trout population increase, with implementation triggers developed in consultation with the Arizona Game and Fish Department (AZGFD) and other stakeholders based on that year's resource conditions.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; response to comment 3.6 (Support Careful Testing of TMFs), near line 1709

supporting_evidence.summary: Because prolonged droughts (paleoclimate tree-ring records show 15-20 year droughts) could lower Lake Powell storage and raise dam release temperatures, increasing nonnative-fish predation risk to humpback chub, Reclamation committed, per the Shortage Guidelines biological opinion, to monitor and control nonnative fish as necessary through the AMP if such warming occurs.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Environmental Baseline, near character offset 111,200 (lines 1663-1665)

supporting_evidence.summary: Reduced Lake Powell storage, by warming Glen Canyon Dam releases, has been identified as a risk pathway for increased nonnative-fish predation and competition pressure on humpback chub. River warming that occurred from 2003 to 2011 (and again in 2014), resulting from reduced Lake Powell storage, was intended to benefit native humpback chub, but the Grand Canyon Ecosystem Model predicted that nonnative fish would also benefit, potentially increasing predation/competition risk to humpback chub through greater fish interactions in critical river segments (RES-014-06). Consistent with this risk pathway, the 2008 Final Biological Opinion notes that because prolonged droughts (paleoclimate tree-ring records show droughts of 15-20 years) could lower Lake Powell storage and raise dam release temperatures, increasing nonnative predation risk to humpback chub, Reclamation committed to monitor and control nonnative fish as necessary through the Adaptive Management Program if such warming occurs (OFF-012-18).

As part of the 2002-2004 experimental program, Reclamation implemented non-native fish suppression releases from Glen Canyon Dam with daily fluctuations of 5,000-20,000 cfs during January 1-March 31 of 2003, continuing this high-fluctuation suppression flow pattern in 2004 and 2005 to test its effectiveness at limiting non-native fish recruitment (EU-LP-OFF-011-14). Consistent with this, non-native fish suppression flows with daily fluctuations between 142 and 566 cubic meters per second -- the metric equivalent of 5,000-20,000 cfs -- were released each January through March from 2003 to 2005, representing a departure from the standard LTEMP/MLFF flow regime (EU-LP-RES-018-06).

Trout Management Flows (TMFs) under LTEMP Alternative D consist of repeated fluctuation cycles combining sustained high flows (e.g., 20,000 cfs, for 2 days to 1 week) with a rapid drop to a very low flow (e.g., 5,000-8,000 cfs), intended to strand young-of-year trout; up to three TMF cycles per month may be tested over as many as four months (May-August). Under the LTEMP preferred alternative, TMFs are triggered by the prediction of high recruitment of young-of-year rainbow trout at Lees Ferry, regardless of the cause of the trout population increase, with the specific implementation triggers developed each year in consultation with the Arizona Game and Fish Department (AZGFD) and other stakeholders based on that year's resource conditions.

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The EU set does not quantify how effective the 2003-2005 suppression flows or Trout Management Flows actually were at reducing nonnative predation risk in practice, only that they were implemented to test or pursue that effect; the loop from 'risk identified' to 'risk successfully mitigated' is not closed by this evidence set.
items.operational_implication: A low-storage/warm-release period should be flagged in monitoring and reporting as a compound risk period requiring both temperature and nonnative-fish-suppression tracking, not a temperature check alone.

items.title: From historic peaking operations through 1991 interim criteria to the 1996 MLFF regime
items.operational_question: How and why did Glen Canyon Dam's operating regime change from historic peaking operations, through 1991 interim criteria, to the 1996 Record of Decision's Modified Low Fluctuating Flow regime?
items.synthesis_claim: Glen Canyon Dam moved from an unrestricted hydroelectric peaking regime to a tightly restricted 1991 interim-criteria regime, and then to the 1996 ROD's Modified Low Fluctuating Flow regime, which restored some of the power flexibility cut in 1991 (raising the up-ramp rate and maximum release) while still holding fluctuations well below historic peaking levels, explicitly to protect downstream resources.
items.scope_and_conditions: Covers the transition from pre-1991 peaking operations through the November 1991 interim operating criteria to the February 1996 Record of Decision; later revisions under LTEMP Alternative D are addressed in SC-LP-004.

analysis_chain.statement: Glen Canyon Dam historically operated in a hydroelectric peaking mode, with releases capable of reaching the powerplant's turbine capacity and no formal daily-fluctuation cap.

Effective November 1, 1991, Reclamation adopted interim operating criteria cutting the maximum peak release from 31,500 cfs to 20,000 cfs, restricting daily fluctuations to 5,000-8,000 cfs, and capping ramp rates at 2,500 cfs/hour (up) and 1,500 cfs/hour (down), while still meeting the 8.23 maf minimum annual release.

analysis_chain.stage: changed rule in the final ROD
analysis_chain.statement: Between the draft and final EIS, the up-ramp rate limit was raised from 2,500 to 4,000 cfs/hour and the maximum allowable release was raised from 20,000 to 25,000 cfs, specifically to enhance power-production flexibility in response to public comments, and the 1996 ROD then formally selected MLFF with these final figures.

MLFF became Glen Canyon Dam's operating regime from 1996 onward, replacing peaking operations and explicitly reducing daily flow fluctuations well below historic peaking levels to protect or enhance downstream resources, and was carried forward as the LTEMP baseline in 2016.

supporting_evidence.summary: Modified Low Fluctuating Flows became the dam's operating regime in 1996, replacing hydroelectric peaking operations, and was the preferred alternative identified in the 1995 Environmental Impact Statement as an adaptive strategy for improving downstream Colorado River ecosystem resources.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Introduction section

supporting_evidence.summary: Beginning November 1, 1991, Reclamation implemented interim operating criteria for Glen Canyon Dam that cut the approved maximum peak release from 31,500 cfs to 20,000 cfs, restricted daily fluctuations to a range of 5,000-8,000 cfs, and capped ramp rates at 2,500 cfs/hour increasing and 1,500 cfs/hour decreasing, while still meeting the 8.23-million-acre-foot minimum annual release.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Chapter 1 Introduction, interim dam operations section (~p. 21)

supporting_evidence.summary: Between the draft and final EIS, the Glen Canyon Dam upramp rate limit was increased from 2,500 to 4,000 cubic feet per second per hour, and the maximum allowable release was increased from 20,000 to 25,000 cubic feet per second, to enhance power production flexibility.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Section II Decision

supporting_evidence.summary: The Secretary selected the Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) Alternative as Glen Canyon Dam's operating criteria, reducing daily flow fluctuations well below historic ("no action") levels while providing high steady releases of short duration to protect or enhance downstream resources and allow limited flexibility for power operations.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Section II Decision

supporting_evidence.summary: Beginning November 1, 1991, Reclamation implemented interim operating criteria for Glen Canyon Dam that cut the approved maximum peak release from 31,500 cfs to 20,000 cfs, restricted daily fluctuations to a range of 5,000-8,000 cfs, and capped ramp rates at 2,500 cfs/hour increasing and 1,500 cfs/hour decreasing, while still meeting the 8.23 maf minimum annual release. Between the draft and final EIS that led to the 1996 Record of Decision, these same starting values were revised: the up-ramp rate limit was increased from 2,500 to 4,000 cfs/hour, and the maximum allowable release was increased from 20,000 to 25,000 cfs, specifically to enhance power production flexibility in response to public comments.

In the 1996 Record of Decision, the Secretary selected the Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) Alternative as Glen Canyon Dam's operating criteria, explicitly because it would reduce daily flow fluctuations well below the 'no action' (historic peaking) levels of releases while providing high steady releases of short duration to protect or enhance downstream resources, allowing limited flexibility for power operations. A peer-reviewed research paper confirms MLFF became the dam's operating regime in 1996, replacing hydroelectric peaking operations, and was the preferred alternative identified in the 1995 Environmental Impact Statement as an adaptive strategy for improving downstream Colorado River ecosystem resources.

Two sources describe the origin of the interim operating criteria that were later adopted as the Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) regime via the 1996 Record of Decision, but they give different establishment dates. Reclamation's 2002 Report to Congress states the Secretary adopted interim operating criteria in November 1991 limiting Glen Canyon Dam minimum/maximum flows and daily fluctuations, later superseded by final operating criteria signed February 1997 (62 Fed. Reg. 9447) that cap releases at 25,000 cfs except during high inflow years or power system emergencies. A USGS historical data report instead states the 1996 ROD adopted, with slight modification, interim operating criteria established in August 1991 as the MLFF alternative. This date discrepancy (August vs. November 1991) is preserved here rather than resolved, since the underlying source excerpts do not clarify whether they refer to the same milestone (e.g., proposal versus formal Secretarial adoption).

items.uncertainty_or_exception: KC-LP-REG-14 documents an unresolved discrepancy over exactly when the interim criteria were established: the 2002 Report to Congress states November 1991, while a USGS historical-data report states August 1991. This card follows the November 1991 date (consistent with the 1997 GAO report lineage used here) but the discrepancy is not resolved by the underlying evidence.
items.operational_implication: Distinguishes three sequential and legally distinct regimes (peaking / 1991 interim / 1996 MLFF) that a knowledge base should not conflate when answering historical questions about what rules applied in a given year.

items.title: Sustained basin drought layers a 2024-2026 emergency drought-response regime on top of the MLFF/Interim Guidelines baseline
items.operational_question: How and why has an emergency drought-response regime (Section 6.E reduced releases, DROA invocation, and elevation-stepped ROW operating guidance) been layered onto the standing MLFF/LTEMP/2007-Interim-Guidelines baseline between 2024 and 2026?
items.synthesis_claim: The 2000-2022 period, the driest 23-year stretch in over a century of record, drove system storage down and produced a near-record-low WY2026 inflow forecast; this sustained drought prompted new, elevation-triggered emergency authorities (the 2024 near-term agreement's Section 6.E release-reduction authority and the 2024 interim ROW operating guidance) that in 2026 were actually invoked to cut the Glen Canyon release from 7.48 to 6.00 maf and pair it with a DROA-triggered Flaming Gorge release -- an emergency regime that supplements, rather than replaces, the standing MLFF/Interim Guidelines framework.
items.scope_and_conditions: Covers the 2007 Interim Guidelines/LTEMP baseline through the 2024 near-term consensus agreement and its 2026 real-time application; the underlying 2007 Interim Guidelines and LTEMP remain the default framework absent this emergency trigger.

analysis_chain.statement: Under the 2007 Interim Guidelines and LTEMP, Lake Powell releases were set by the four-tier structure (the Mid-Elevation Release Tier producing 7.48 or 8.23 maf depending on Lake Mead's elevation), with MLFF/LTEMP governing only the sub-annual release pattern.

The 2000-2022 period was the driest 23-year stretch in over a century of record (and among the driest in 1,200 years), with total system storage falling 3.37 maf during WY2025 alone, and WY2026 inflow forecast near-record-low.

This sustained drought prompted the 2024 near-term consensus agreement's new Section XI.G.6.E authority (triggering planning to cut releases to not less than 6.0 maf if Powell is projected below 3,500 ft), plus a 2024 interim operating guidance imposing elevation-stepped ROW conduit flow limits and a 3,490 ft operating target.

Interior invoked Section 6.E to cut the WY2026 release from 7.48 to 6.00 maf and paired it with a DROA-triggered 660,000 acre-foot to 1 maf Flaming Gorge release, explicitly to keep Lake Powell above 3,500 ft through April 2027.

This emergency regime layers a new, elevation-triggered emergency-reduction authority and infrastructure-protection guidance on top of the existing MLFF/Interim Guidelines framework, which remains the default absent a further trigger, consistent with Reclamation's own concern about enhanced reliance on the river outlet works prompting the 2024 guidance.

supporting_evidence.summary: In the Mid-Elevation Release Tier (Lake Powell January 1 elevation projected below 3,575 feet and at or above 3,525 feet), the Secretary releases 7.48 maf from Lake Powell if Lake Mead's January 1 elevation is at or above 1,025 feet, or 8.23 maf if Lake Mead is below 1,025 feet.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Section 6.C Mid-Elevation Release Tier

supporting_evidence.summary: The annual volume of water released from Glen Canyon Dam under the LTEMP is determined by the Long-Range Operating Criteria (LROC) as currently implemented through the 2007 Interim Guidelines until 2026; guidelines for annual releases after 2026 will be determined under a separate process under the terms of the 2007 Guidelines.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Section 1.5 Scope of the EIS

supporting_evidence.summary: The period from 2000 through 2022 is the driest 23-year period in more than a century and one of the driest periods in the last 1,200 years in the Colorado River Basin.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; III. Background

supporting_evidence.summary: The Colorado River Basin's total system storage decreased by 3.37 maf during water year 2025, falling from 43 percent to 37 percent of capacity; the period from 2000 through 2022 represents the lowest 23-year inflow in the historic record and one of the lowest in the past 1,200 years.

supporting_evidence.summary: Inflows into Lake Powell in 2026 are projected to be the lowest ever measured, breaking the previous record set in 2002, driven by a downward snowpack trend and a March 2026 heat wave that was the most extreme on record in the Southwest for that time of year.

supporting_evidence.summary: Lake Powell's water year 2026 minimum probable inflow is forecasted at just 2.78 million acre-feet, 29 percent of the historical average and one of the lowest on record, with Reclamation's April 24-Month Study projecting Lake Powell may decline below 3,490 ft (minimum power pool) by August 2026 without major intervention.

supporting_evidence.summary: Under the 2024 near-term consensus agreement, reduced Glen Canyon Dam releases to the Lower Basin are allowed if Lake Powell elevations drop below 3,500 feet, permitting 6.0 MAF releases instead of the 7.0 MAF previously agreed under the 2007 Interim Guidelines.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Near-Term Operations: 2024 Supplemental Environmental Impact Statement

supporting_evidence.summary: Under the 2024 ROD's new Section XI.G.6.E, if the minimum probable 24-Month Study projects an elevation below 3,500 feet at Lake Powell in the next 12 months, the Secretary must begin planning to reduce Lake Powell releases as needed to not less than 6.0 MAF for the Water Year to maintain elevation 3,500 feet.

supporting_evidence.summary: To limit cavitation risk in the river outlet works at low reservoir levels, Reclamation set interim maximum per-conduit flow limits below the 3,750 cfs design maximum, stepping down with elevation - e.g., 3,185 cfs at elevation 3,490 ft, 2,200 cfs at 3,420 ft, 1,200 cfs at 3,400 ft, and 0 cfs at 3,390 ft.
