supporting_evidence.summary: Because historically dry WY2026 conditions caused Lake Powell to be projected to decline below elevation 3,500 feet, the Department of the Interior invoked Section 6.E of the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS ROD to reduce Lake Powell's annual release from 7.48 maf to 6.00 maf, coupled with a 2026 Drought Response Operations Plan releasing approximately 660,000 to 1.00 maf of additional water from Flaming Gorge Reservoir to Lake Powell by April 2027.

supporting_evidence.summary: To stabilize Lake Powell in 2026, Reclamation plans to add about 2.48 million acre-feet by releasing 660,000 to 1 million acre-feet from Flaming Gorge Reservoir (under the 2019 Drought Response Operating Agreements, April 2026-April 2027) and by reducing the Lake Powell-to-Lake Mead annual release volume from 7.48 maf to 6.0 maf through September 2026 under Section 6E of the 2024 SEIS Record of Decision, together expected to raise Lake Powell's elevation about 54 ft to at least 3,500 ft by April 2027.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; news release body

supporting_evidence.summary: With the consent of the four Upper Basin states, Reclamation will release between 660,000 and 1 million acre-feet from Flaming Gorge Reservoir (82 percent full) into Lake Powell over the 12 months following the April 2026 announcement, building on a smaller 463,000-acre-foot release used to prop up Powell in 2022-23.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; article body

supporting_evidence.summary: Since the Draft SEIS, Reclamation identified enhanced risks associated with relying on Glen Canyon Dam's river outlet works as the exclusive means of releasing water at low reservoir elevations for sustained periods, prompting the 2024 Interim Operating Guidance for Low Reservoir Levels.
supporting_evidence.source_location: extracted text; Chapter 1.9 Operational Considerations

supporting_evidence.summary: Under the 2024 near-term consensus agreement / 2024 ROD's new Section XI.G.6.E (per CRS summary and the official Record of Decision), if the minimum probable 24-Month Study projects an elevation below 3,500 feet at Lake Powell in the next 12 months, the Secretary must begin planning to reduce Lake Powell releases as needed to not less than 6.0 maf for the Water Year to maintain elevation 3,500 feet -- in lieu of a 7.0 maf figure referenced under the near-term proposal framing.

Under the Upper Basin DCP's DROA, Upper Basin states agreed to operate system units to keep Lake Powell's surface above elevation 3,525 feet, 35 feet above minimum power pool (EU-LP-CRS-001-04). Reclamation's stated operational goal under DROA is to 'protect' this 3,525-ft elevation, primarily via reduced Glen Canyon Dam releases and drawdown of upstream initial-unit reservoirs (EU-LP-CRS-002-04). The DROA establishes the process for Reclamation, in collaboration with the Upper Basin States, to release additional water from upstream CRSP initial-unit reservoirs (Flaming Gorge, Aspinall, Navajo, Glen Canyon/Lake Powell) to reduce the risk of Lake Powell reaching critical elevation (EU-LP-OFF-017-03). In CRSS modeling, Powell Infrastructure Protection (PIP) releases from the Upper Initial Units (Flaming Gorge, Blue Mesa, Navajo) are specifically triggered when Lake Powell is projected to fall below elevation 3,525 feet (EU-LP-OFF-021-06). This target was actually invoked when the July 2025 24-Month Study projected Lake Powell declining below the 3,525.00-ft DROA target elevation, triggering DROA year-2025 drought-response planning under the DCP-related agreements (EU-LP-OFF-022-03); consistent with protecting this same target, the December 2025 24-Month Study reduced Glen Canyon Dam's monthly release volumes for December 2025 through April 2026 by 0.598 maf (EU-LP-OFF-023-03).

On April 17, 2026, the Bureau of Reclamation announced unprecedented actions to store more water in Lake Powell -- then less than 25 percent full -- to preserve hydropower generation and protect Glen Canyon Dam water-delivery infrastructure the agency said was at risk from low reservoir levels (EU-LP-MED-001-01). With the consent of the four Upper Basin states, Reclamation committed to releasing between 660,000 and 1 million acre-feet from Flaming Gorge Reservoir (82 percent full) into Lake Powell over the 12 months following the announcement, building on a smaller 463,000-acre-foot release used to prop up Powell in 2022-23 (EU-LP-MED-001-02). Because WY2026 was historically dry and Lake Powell was projected to decline below elevation 3,500 feet, the Department of the Interior invoked Section 6.E of the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS ROD to reduce Lake Powell's annual release from 7.48 maf to 6.00 maf, coupled with a 2026 Drought Response Operations Plan releasing approximately 660,000 to 1.00 maf of additional water from Flaming Gorge Reservoir to Lake Powell by April 2027 (EU-LP-OFF-023-02). Reclamation's newsroom release confirms the combined plan: adding about 2.48 million acre-feet via the 660,000 AF-1 maf Flaming Gorge release (April 2026-April 2027, under the 2019 Drought Response Operating Agreements) plus the 7.48-to-6.0-maf release reduction through September 2026 under Section 6E, together expected to raise Lake Powell's elevation about 54 feet to at least 3,500 feet by April 2027 (EU-LP-OFF-035-02).

Reclamation's original Technical Record of Design and Construction established elevation 3,490 ft as the minimum reservoir elevation for power production, 20 ft above the penstock intake centerline (elevation 3,470 ft); water cannot be released through the penstocks below 3,490 ft (OFF-025-03). Multiple later sources restate this same threshold: Reclamation estimates the depth for minimum power pool is 20 ft above the penstocks, i.e. elevation 3,490 fasl (CRS-002-02); at 3,490 ft, minimum power pool is 20 ft above the generators' actual penstock intakes, and the dam's eight turbines must be shut down at minimum power pool to avoid cavitation (MED-002-01); the 1999 multi-level intake structure hydraulic model study likewise designates elevation 3,490 ft as the minimum water surface for power operations (OFF-028-06); the 2016 LTEMP Final EIS states hydropower production would cease if Lake Powell drops below approximately 3,490 ft (OFF-005-01); the 2024 Near-term Operations SEIS ROD notes dry hydrology in recent years produced low Lake Powell elevations at levels such as 3,490 ft, giving Reclamation operating experience at this threshold (OFF-002-06); the 2024 LTEMP Final Supplemental EIS states Reclamation's Interim Operating Guidance for Low Reservoir Levels directs use of the full extent of Upper Colorado Basin operational capabilities to try to keep Lake Powell at or above elevation 3,490 ft (OFF-007-03); and an April 2026 status report reiterates that hydropower generation stops at 3,490 feet, with the reservoir at 3,526 feet at that time and Reclamation aiming to keep it above 3,500 feet (MED-001-04).

The river outlet works (four 96-inch-diameter steel pipes) were designed with an unrestricted capacity of 3,750 cfs per tube (15,000 cfs total) at reservoir elevation 3,490 ft (minimum power-operation water surface). Below elevation 3,550 ft, however, the 2024 LTEMP Final SEIS's modeling assumed a reduced capacity of 3,150 cfs per tube (12,600 cfs total) rather than the unrestricted 3,750 cfs/tube maximum. Separately, Reclamation's March 2024 interim operating guidance set even more granular, elevation-stepped interim maximum per-conduit flow limits to limit cavitation risk, including 3,185 cfs at elevation 3,490 ft, stepping down to 2,200 cfs at 3,420 ft, 1,200 cfs at 3,400 ft, and 0 cfs at 3,390 ft.

When Lake Powell drops below the minimum power pool elevation of 3,490 feet, Glen Canyon Dam can no longer release water through its powerplant turbines/penstocks and must rely on the river outlet works (ROW), whose capacity is limited and increases with pool elevation (OFF-021-08); the Post-2026 Draft EIS states the dam 'was not envisioned to operate below minimum power pool (elevation 3,490 feet)' and that below this elevation water must be released through the jet tubes at the end of the ROW instead of the penstocks (OFF-019-05). Across all anticipated post-2026 operating alternatives, releases from Lake Powell may fall below the alternative's specified release volume at elevations below 3,490 feet due to this infrastructure limitation (OFF-020-04). A separate study quantified the resulting shortfall: at elevation 3,430 feet, the ROW can discharge only 10,200 cfs (7.41 MAF/year), considerably less than the Law of the River's 8.23 MAF/year delivery requirement, and below the ROW's own elevation of 3,370 feet, approximately 1.89 MAF becomes inaccessible dead storage (CRS-002-08).

Multiple sources indicate the river outlet works (ROW) were not designed for, and cannot be fully relied upon for, long-term or high-flow releases at low Lake Powell levels. Reclamation's 2024 Technical Decision Memorandum found no design reference indicating the ROW were intended for long-term water conveyance at low reservoir levels; historically they were used only to augment powerplant/spillway discharges for short durations (e.g., about three months during 1983 flood releases, days to a week for high-flow experiments) (OFF-025-04). A 2023 special inspection found the hollow-jet valves, pipes, and ring-follower gates sufficient for periodic/seasonal releases but flagged concern about long-term high-flow use and recommended a major overhaul or replacement for high confidence in continuous long-term operation (OFF-025-05). This concern has historical precedent: on April 20, 1965, at reservoir elevation 3,490 ft with the ROW variably open, the dam's tailrace stabilization slab was undermined by a recirculating eddy from ROW operation and portions of it collapsed, because tailwater was 4-6 feet lower than had been predicted by physical modeling (OFF-025-06). More recently, in 2023, when the ROW were used for a high-flow release into the Grand Canyon at low-reservoir levels, damaging cavitation occurred, and the Bureau has warned further extended use would likely cause more (MED-002-03). Based on this evidence, Reclamation's formal conclusion is that it should not rely on the ROW as the sole means of releasing water from Glen Canyon Dam, as would be required below minimum power pool (3,490 ft), given current uncertainty about long-term conduit and hollow-jet valve performance and tailrace sedimentation (OFF-025-07).

Two independent Reclamation documents state the identical drought-severity statistic: the period from 2000 through 2022 was the driest/lowest 23-year period in more than a century of record and one of the driest/lowest such periods in the last 1,200 years in the Colorado River Basin. The 2024 Near-term Colorado River Operations SEIS Record of Decision cites this as the basis for supplementing the 2007 Interim Guidelines (OFF-002-07), and the Draft 2026 Annual Operating Plan restates the same statistic while separately reporting that total system storage fell by 3.37 MAF during water year 2025, from 43 percent to 37 percent of capacity (OFF-022-07).

items.uncertainty_or_exception: KC-LP-OPR-13 preserves an unreconciled framing difference between a CRS description of a prior '7.0 MAF' baseline being replaced and the ROD's 'not less than 6.0 maf' planning-floor language; this card follows the ROD's framing as authoritative for the 6.0 maf figure.
items.operational_implication: Shows the current emergency regime is additive and triggered, not a wholesale replacement of MLFF/Interim Guidelines; a report or index should present 2026 operations as 'baseline framework plus active emergency trigger,' not as a new standalone regime.

items.title: September 2005 dissolved-oxygen violation caused by low-elevation stratification
items.operational_question: What was the September 2005 Glen Canyon Dam dissolved-oxygen violation, what caused it, and what does it reveal about a low-elevation operational failure mode distinct from power/release-capacity limits?
items.synthesis_claim: In September 2005, Glen Canyon Dam tailwater dissolved oxygen fell below EPA cold-water-fishery criteria because historically low reservoir elevations placed the reservoir's low-oxygen metalimnetic layer directly at the penstock withdrawal elevation, allowing oxygen-depleted water to be exported through the dam -- a documented water-quality failure mode tied specifically to low reservoir elevation.
items.scope_and_conditions: Single documented event, September 2005, at Glen Canyon Dam tailwater; based on a CE-QUAL-W2 reservoir-quality modeling study.

analysis_chain.statement: In most years, the reservoir's metalimnetic oxygen-minimum layer sits well above the penstock withdrawal elevation (3,470 ft), so oxygen-depleted water does not reach the dam's discharge.

In 2005, reservoir elevations were the lowest since initial filling, which placed the low-dissolved-oxygen metalimnetic layer just above the penstock elevation, letting an oxygen-depleted plume be captured in the penstock withdrawal zone and exported through the dam.

Tailwater dissolved oxygen dropped below 4.0 mg/L in September 2005, violating the EPA cold-water-fishery dissolved-oxygen criteria (1-day mean minimum 4.0 mg/L) and raising concern for the cold-water fishery below the dam.

This event demonstrates that low reservoir elevation is a structural vulnerability for water-quality performance, not just water-quantity or power performance, because withdrawal-zone water quality depends on how reservoir thermal/oxygen stratification lines up with the fixed penstock elevation.

supporting_evidence.summary: In most years the metalimnetic oxygen minimum does not affect dam discharges because it sits well above the penstock elevation (3,470 ft), but in 2005 reservoir elevations were the lowest since initial filling and the low-DO metalimnetic water was located just above the penstock elevation, allowing oxygen-depleted water to pass through the dam.

items.title: Early sediment-redistribution flow tests (1997, 2000) failed to build sandbars, for two distinct reasons
items.operational_question: What early post-dam sediment-redistribution flow experiments failed to achieve their sandbar-building objectives, why did each fail, and how did these failures relate to the later HFE protocol redesign?
items.synthesis_claim: Two early post-dam sediment-redistribution flow experiments predating the current HFE protocol -- the November 1997 Test Flow and the 2000 Low Summer Steady Flow Experiment -- failed to achieve their sandbar-building objectives for two different documented reasons (insufficient release magnitude versus insufficient antecedent sediment supply), a pattern of failure consistent with the post-2012 protocol's redesign to explicitly time releases to tributary sand inputs rather than a fixed schedule.
items.scope_and_conditions: Covers the November 1997 Test Flow and the 2000 Low Summer Steady Flow Experiment, both predating the 2012 sediment-triggered HFE protocol described in SC-LP-002.

analysis_chain.statement: Both the November 1997 Test Flow (a constant 872 m3/s release for 48 hours) and the 2000 Low Summer Steady Flow Experiment (a 4-day 864 m3/s pulse, 3 months at a constant 227 m3/s, then a 4-day 881 m3/s pulse) were designed to redistribute channel sediment into rebuilt sandbars.
The Test Flow did not significantly aggrade sandbars because its magnitude was insufficient to distribute sand to open depositional locations at higher elevations.

The Low Summer Steady Flow produced minimal sandbar building because the Paria River had supplied very little antecedent sediment, and the sustained low steady discharge instead allowed invasive tamarisk seedlings to colonize the exposed bare sand deposits.

These two failures, for two different root causes, are consistent with the later post-2012 protocol's redesign to explicitly time HFE releases to follow documented tributary sand inputs rather than run on a fixed schedule.

supporting_evidence.summary: Two early post-dam sediment-redistribution flow experiments, predating the LTEMP HFE protocol, failed to achieve their sandbar-building objectives, each for a different reason. The November 3, 1997 Test Flow (a constant 872 m3/s release for 48 hours), Reclamation's first attempt at a post-tributary-flood sediment-redistribution release, did not significantly aggrade sandbars because its magnitude was insufficient to distribute sand to open depositional locations at higher elevations (RES-018-09). The 2000 Low Summer Steady Flow Experiment (a 4-day 864 m3/s release, 3 months of constant 227 m3/s, then a 4-day 881 m3/s release) produced minimal sandbar building because the Paria River had supplied very little sediment beforehand, and the sustained low, steady discharge instead allowed proliferation of invasive tamarisk seedlings on bare sand deposits (RES-018-10).

High flow experiments were tested in 1996, 1997, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2013, and 2014 to rebuild eroded sandbars; since 2012 a 10-year protocol implements one to two high flow experiments annually, timed to follow tributary sand inputs from the Paria River in fall and/or spring (EU-LP-RES-014-05). This decision-making protocol, approved by the Department of the Interior in 2012, coordinates dam releases to occur following large sand inputs delivered to the Colorado River by a major tributary (EU-LP-RES-018-01). Across the full historical record, 11 HFEs were released from Glen Canyon Dam between 1996 and November 2018, with peak magnitudes ranging from 864 to 1,274 cubic meters per second and durations from 24 to 168 hours, including lower-magnitude habitat maintenance flows (HMFs) in 1997 and 2000 (EU-LP-RES-018-02).

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The EU set does not explicitly state that these 1997/2000 failures were a directly named cause of the 2012 protocol redesign; the sequential timing and shared objective make the connection plausible but it is inferred here, not source-confirmed as an explicit causal statement.
items.operational_implication: Supports treating sediment-supply timing as the single most important design variable for HFE effectiveness, ahead of release magnitude alone.

items.title: Projected elevation-recovery consequence of the 2026 emergency drought-response package
items.operational_question: What projected consequence do Reclamation's 2026 emergency drought-response actions (the Section 6.E release reduction plus the DROA Flaming Gorge release) have on Lake Powell's elevation trajectory?
items.synthesis_claim: Reclamation projects that its combined 2026 drought-response package -- reducing the WY2026 Glen Canyon release from 7.48 to 6.00 maf and releasing 660,000 acre-feet to 1 maf from Flaming Gorge Reservoir into Lake Powell by April 2027 -- will raise Lake Powell's elevation by about 54 feet, to at least 3,500 feet, by April 2027, starting from an April 2026 minimum-probable forecast that had projected a possible decline below the 3,490 ft minimum power pool by August 2026 absent intervention.
items.scope_and_conditions: A forward-looking (projected, not yet observed) outcome as stated in Reclamation's April 2026 newsroom release, contingent on realized WY2026-2027 hydrology and full delivery of the stated Flaming Gorge release.

analysis_chain.statement: Reclamation's April 2026 minimum-probable 24-Month Study forecast Lake Powell's WY2026 minimum probable inflow at just 2.78 maf (29 percent of historical average, one of the lowest on record), and projected Lake Powell could decline below 3,490 ft (minimum power pool) by August 2026 without major intervention.

Interior invoked Section 6.E of the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS ROD to cut the WY2026 Glen Canyon release from 7.48 to 6.00 maf, and, with the consent of the four Upper Basin states, committed to releasing 660,000 acre-feet to 1 maf from Flaming Gorge Reservoir into Lake Powell between April 2026 and April 2027.

Reclamation's newsroom release states the combined package -- about 2.48 million acre-feet added via the Flaming Gorge release plus the release reduction -- is expected to raise Lake Powell's elevation by about 54 feet, to at least 3,500 feet, by April 2027.

This is an explicitly projected, not yet observed, outcome contingent on future hydrology; the same evidence set documents that 2021-2022 DROA-triggered upstream release volumes were reported inconsistently across sources, underscoring that even the accounting of past DROA actions has had reconciliation gaps.

supporting_evidence.summary: Lake Powell's water year 2026 minimum probable inflow is forecasted at just 2.78 million acre-feet, 29 percent of the historical average and one of the lowest on record, with Reclamation's April 24-Month Study projecting Lake Powell may decline below 3,490 ft (minimum power pool) by August 2026 without major intervention.

supporting_evidence.summary: On April 17, 2026, the Bureau of Reclamation announced unprecedented actions to store more water in Lake Powell -- then less than 25 percent full -- to preserve hydropower generation and protect Glen Canyon Dam water-delivery infrastructure the agency said was at risk from low reservoir levels (EU-LP-MED-001-01). With the consent of the four Upper Basin states, Reclamation committed to releasing between 660,000 and 1 million acre-feet from Flaming Gorge Reservoir (82 percent full) into Lake Powell over the 12 months following the announcement, building on a smaller 463,000-acre-foot release used to prop up Powell in 2022-23 (EU-LP-MED-001-02). Because WY2026 was historically dry and Lake Powell was projected to decline below elevation 3,500 feet, the Department of the Interior invoked Section 6.E of the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS ROD to reduce Lake Powell's annual release from 7.48 maf to 6.00 maf, coupled with a 2026 Drought Response Operations Plan releasing approximately 660,000 to 1.00 maf of additional water from Flaming Gorge Reservoir to Lake Powell by April 2027 (EU-LP-OFF-023-02). Reclamation's newsroom release confirms the combined plan: adding about 2.48 million acre-feet via the 660,000 AF-1 maf Flaming Gorge release (April 2026-April 2027, under the 2019 Drought Response Operating Agreements) plus the 7.48-to-6.0-maf release reduction through September 2026 under Section 6E, together expected to raise Lake Powell's elevation about 54 feet to at least 3,500 feet by April 2027 (EU-LP-OFF-035-02).

Circle of Blue reporting (April 2026) states inflows into Lake Powell in 2026 are projected to be the lowest ever measured, breaking the previous record set in 2002, driven by a downward snowpack trend and a March 2026 heat wave that was the most extreme on record in the Southwest for that time of year (MED-001-05). Reclamation's newsroom release states Lake Powell's water year 2026 minimum probable inflow is forecasted at just 2.78 million acre-feet, 29 percent of historical average and one of the lowest on record, with Reclamation's April 24-Month Study projecting Lake Powell may decline below 3,490 ft (minimum power pool) by August 2026 without major intervention (OFF-035-01).

CRS R47497 states that in 2021 Reclamation transferred 180,000 acre-feet to Lake Powell from Flaming Gorge (125,000 AF), Blue Mesa (36,000 AF), and Navajo (20,000 AF) reservoirs, and in 2022 reduced Lake Powell releases from 7.48 to 7.00 maf while transferring an additional 0.50 maf from Flaming Gorge (EU-LP-CRS-002-05). Reclamation's own DROA program page states that beginning summer 2021, pursuant to the DROA, Reclamation determined an imminent need to release 161,000 acre-feet from the upstream Flaming Gorge and Aspinall Unit (Blue Mesa) Initial Units, and that in January 2022 it additionally modified Glen Canyon Dam releases, readjusting 350,000 acre-feet, to protect critical elevations at Lake Powell (EU-LP-OFF-031-03). The two sources give different acre-foot totals for what appears to be overlapping 2021-2022 DROA-triggered actions (180,000 AF vs. 161,000 AF for 2021; a 0.50 maf Flaming Gorge transfer vs. a 350,000 AF Glen Canyon Dam release readjustment for 2022), and neither source alone clarifies whether these figures represent the same actions counted differently, partial vs. final tallies, or genuinely distinct actions.

items.uncertainty_or_exception: This projection depends on the full 660,000 AF-1 maf Flaming Gorge range actually being delivered on the stated schedule and on no further hydrologic deterioration; the evidence set does not include a subsequent (post-April-2026) 24-Month Study confirming whether the projected 54-foot rise was realized.
items.operational_implication: This card should be revisited once later 2026-2027 24-Month Studies are available, to convert it from a projected to an observed consequence, and to check the Flaming Gorge release volume actually delivered against the 660,000 AF-1 maf commitment.
items.source_verification_note: Rereading confirmed the projected-outcome wording verbatim in OFF-035: the combined actions are 'expected to raise Lake Powell's elevation about 54 feet, to at least 3,500 feet, by April 2027.' This is explicitly forward-looking language ('expected'), which is why evidence_depth/consequence_basis are marked as a projection rather than an observed result.

items.title: Observed HFE effectiveness diverges structurally by sandbar type over the long-term monitoring record
items.operational_question: What observed long-term consequence has the post-1996 HFE protocol had on different types of Grand Canyon sandbars, based on the 45-site long-term monitoring network?
items.synthesis_claim: The 45-site long-term sandbar monitoring network shows the HFE protocol produced measurable short-term sandbar growth immediately following the 2012-2014 HFEs, but its long-term consequence diverges structurally by bar type: wide reattachment bars and upper pool deposits can now at best only replace sediment eroded between events due to vegetation-driven channel narrowing, while separation and undifferentiated eddy bars have not been durably rebuilt at all because rapid erosion at these unvegetated, wind-exposed sites outpaces each HFE's gains.
items.scope_and_conditions: Covers HFEs released 1996-2018 and monitored through the 45-site long-term sandbar network and its associated methodology (topographic surveys through 2011-era HFEs, then remote photography plus delayed annual surveys for 2012-2018 HFEs).

analysis_chain.statement: The HFE protocol released 11 HFEs between 1996 and November 2018, at peak magnitudes of 864-1,274 m3/s and durations of 24-168 hours, explicitly to mobilize channel sediment into sandbars.

At the 45-site monitoring network, sandbars were measured as larger at 52 percent, 52 percent, and 57 percent of sites immediately following the 2012, 2013, and 2014 HFEs respectively, with total sand volume at these sites increasing over the program's first four years.

At wide reattachment bars and upper pool deposits, vegetation stabilization and vertical aggradation have progressively narrowed the channel and reduced available accommodation space, so at best HFEs can only replace sediment eroded between events rather than produce net growth; at separation bars and undifferentiated eddy bars, HFEs have not effectively rebuilt the bars, which continue to gradually decrease in volume because rapid erosion at these unvegetated, wind-exposed sites outpaces each HFE's gains.

The 45-site network represents only 7-9 percent of all sandbars in Marble and Grand Canyons (though shown representative of system-wide average response), and its measurement methodology shifted mid-program (from topographic survey to remote photography plus delayed annual surveys for the 2012-2018 HFEs), so confidence in any single-bar-type trend should be weighed against this partial coverage and methodology change.

supporting_evidence.summary: Glen Canyon Dam's High-Flow Experiment (HFE) protocol effectiveness is tracked through a network of 45 long-term sandbar monitoring sites, part of a larger repeat topographic/bathymetric survey program (approximately 1,800 surveys) that represents only 7-9 percent of all sandbars in Marble and Grand Canyons but has been shown, by comparison with larger samples, to consistently characterize system-wide average sandbar response. At these 45 sites, sandbars were measured as larger at 52%, 52%, and 57% of sites immediately following the 2012, 2013, and 2014 HFEs respectively, with total sand volume at these sites increasing over the program's first 4 years. For the five HFEs released between 2012 and 2018, pre/post-event topographic surveys were not conducted; instead sandbar response was assessed via daily repeat photographs from remote automated cameras plus annual monitoring surveys collected approximately 11 months after each event.

The long-term effectiveness of the High-Flow Experiment (HFE) protocol at rebuilding Grand Canyon sandbars differs by bar type and has structural limits at both ends. At wide reattachment bars and upper pool deposits, vegetation stabilization and vertical aggradation during successive HFEs have progressively narrowed the channel and reduced the accommodation space available for further deposition, so at best HFEs can only replace sediment eroded during normal dam operations between events rather than produce net growth (RES-018-12). At separation bars and undifferentiated eddy bars, HFEs have not effectively rebuilt the bars, which have continued to gradually decrease in volume over time; although these bars consistently aggrade during individual HFEs, the subsequent erosion at these unvegetated, wind-exposed sites is rapid (RES-018-13).

High flow experiments were tested in 1996, 1997, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2013, and 2014 to rebuild eroded sandbars; since 2012 a 10-year protocol implements one to two high flow experiments annually, timed to follow tributary sand inputs from the Paria River in fall and/or spring (EU-LP-RES-014-05). This decision-making protocol, approved by the Department of the Interior in 2012, coordinates dam releases to occur following large sand inputs delivered to the Colorado River by a major tributary (EU-LP-RES-018-01). Across the full historical record, 11 HFEs were released from Glen Canyon Dam between 1996 and November 2018, with peak magnitudes ranging from 864 to 1,274 cubic meters per second and durations from 24 to 168 hours, including lower-magnitude habitat maintenance flows (HMFs) in 1997 and 2000 (EU-LP-RES-018-02).

items.uncertainty_or_exception: The mid-program shift from topographic surveys to remote photography and delayed annual surveys (for the 2012-2018 HFEs) means the short-term (52-57 percent) and long-term bar-type-specific results are not derived from an identical measurement method throughout the program's history; this should be flagged if these percentages are ever compared across the full historical record.
items.operational_implication: A report claiming HFEs do or do not 'work' should specify which of the two structurally different bar types it means, since the observed consequence is genuinely bifurcated rather than uniform across the monitored sandbar population.
